---
title: "Capstone: Final Group Presentation"
---

The final for this class is a **group presentation (under 10 minutes)** exploring
a plant genetics topic of your group's choice, presented in class on
**December 1 and 3**. Groups are 4–5 people. It's worth 30% of your grade
(100 points, plus up to 5 extra credit).

## Start thinking about it now

The capstone comes at the end, but the best presentations start much
earlier — in two ways.

**The topic.** Ideas will come at you all quarter: a lecture that hooks you,
a reading, the cacao tour, a guest speaker, something you dig up researching
your midterm. When something makes you think "I want to know more about
that," write it down — that list is where good capstone topics come from.
Like the midterm, focused beats broad, and the same three doors apply: a
problem plant genetics can help solve, an open question, or how a genetic
technology works.

**The group.** This is a group project, which makes the class itself part of
the assignment: sit next to someone new, talk during the break, compare
answers during in-class activities. The people you meet in the first weeks
may well become your group — and groups that form around a shared interest
tend to have more fun with this. If you'd rather be assigned to a group,
that's completely fine too; the preference survey (due **Thu Oct 29**) asks
which you want.

## What you submit

- **Presentation file** (PDF or PPTX) — one upload per group on Canvas;
  anyone in the group can submit and it counts for everyone. Due Dec 1 at
  3:10 PM regardless of which day your group presents.
- **Individual contributions statement** — every student submits their own
  short, confidential statement: what you contributed (slides, research,
  figures, organizing, presenting sections…) and how the work was divided.
  A few sentences is plenty. Only the teaching team sees it; it's how we
  make sure credit lands where the work happened.

## What we're looking for

Think of your presentation as a short lecture to the rest of the class.
Your audience has taken the same course you have, so you can assume they
know what an allele, a QTL, or CRISPR is. What they don't know is your
topic. By the end of your talk, they should understand one plant
genetics story well: what the problem or question is, what is known about
the genetics behind it, how researchers figured that out, and what is
still unresolved.

**Go into the genetics.** A presentation that stays at the surface
("drought is a big problem for wheat, and genetics can help") will not score
well on depth. Strong presentations name the genes, alleles,
mutations, or loci involved, explain how they work (the mechanism), and
show the evidence: the experiment, the mapping study, the field trial, the
figure from the paper. If you can say "researchers found X, and we know
this because they did Y," you are at the right depth.

**A shape that works:**

- **Introduction.** The background your audience needs and why the topic
  matters (a crop, a disease, a farmer's problem, a food security issue).
  Keep it short, but don't skip it.
- **Body.** The main portion. What is known about the genetics, how it was
  discovered, and how it is being used or could be used (breeding, gene
  editing, conservation, and so on). Give each slide one take-home message.
- **Conclusion.** Pull the key insights together and end on one clear
  message you want people to remember. Open questions and where the field
  is heading make a good ending.

**Slides.** Use figures, diagrams, and photos instead of walls of text, and
make sure every image is high enough resolution to read from the back of
the room. Put your citations on the slides where the claims are made, so
the audience can see where each fact comes from (at least 5 citations
total, in a consistent format, for papers and websites alike). A references
slide at the end is a good idea too.

**Time.** Under 10 minutes for the whole group, and aim for about 8. Practice
out loud together with a timer, more than once, and cut until you are under
10. Running long cuts into other groups' time, and a very short talk rarely
leaves room to explore the topic in depth.

**Working as a group.** We grade collaboration from how evenly the work was
shared, so build your slides in a shared file (for example Google Slides)
where the edit history shows who did what. Your individual statement should
match what the group did.

**Being in the audience.** Come both days and pay attention to the other
groups. Your group also has an assigned group to ask a question
([see the table above](#questions)), and good questions are part of what
makes these two days fun.

**Extra credit (up to 5 points)** goes to groups that bring something
genuinely their own: an original framing, a creative way of explaining the
genetics, a comparison or synthesis you won't find in a standard review.

## How it's graded {#rubric}

**100 points total, plus up to 5 extra credit.** Most criteria are one grade
for the whole group. Two are graded for each student separately.

| Criterion | Points | Graded for |
|---|---|---|
| Depth of content | 10 | Group |
| Accuracy and relevance | 10 | Group |
| Use of references (at least 5 citations) | 10 | Group |
| Introduction | 5 | Group |
| Body | 10 | Group |
| Conclusion | 5 | Group |
| Clarity and conciseness | 10 | Group |
| Slide design | 10 | Group |
| Collaboration | 10 | Group |
| Time management and communication (under 10 minutes) | 5 | Group |
| Individual contribution (from your statement) | 10 | Each student |
| Audience engagement (attend both days) | 5 | Each student |
| **Total** | **100** | |
| Extra credit: novelty | up to 5 | Group |

The full rubric, with what each level looks like, is [below](#full-rubric). The group grade covers
depth of content, accuracy, use of references (**at least 5 citations** on
your slides), introduction / body / conclusion structure, clarity, slide
design, collaboration, and time management (stay under 10 minutes).
Two pieces are graded per student: your **individual contribution** (from
your statement) and **audience engagement** — being present and engaged
during the other groups' presentations on both days. Up to 5 extra credit points for
genuinely creative insights or framings.

## Full rubric

Scores between levels are possible; the levels are anchors.

(Group grade via the group presentation submission, except Individual
Contribution and Audience Engagement, which are per-student.)

### Depth of Content (10 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | Explores the topic in real depth with clear command of the genetics/genomics involved; goes beyond surface-level description to mechanism and evidence. |
| 7 | Good | Solid coverage with occasional shallow patches or hand-waving on the genetics. |
| 4 | Developing | Mostly surface-level; genetics content is thin or garbled. |
| 0 | Missing | Topic not meaningfully explored. |

### Accuracy and Relevance (10 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | Information is accurate, current, and consistently relevant to the topic. |
| 7 | Good | Largely accurate with minor errors or occasional tangents. |
| 4 | Developing | Multiple factual errors or substantial irrelevant content. |
| 0 | Missing | Unreliable throughout. |

### Use of References (10 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | At least five citations used effectively where claims need support; correct citation format for papers and websites. |
| 7 | Good | Meets the minimum but citations are uneven — some slides make claims without support, or formatting is inconsistent. |
| 4 | Developing | Few citations, or sources not credible. |
| 0 | Missing | No references. |

### Introduction (5 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Excellent | Provides the background the audience needs and sets up why the topic matters before diving in. |
| 3 | Good | Background present but rushed, or the motivation is implied rather than stated. |
| 0 | Missing | Presentation starts mid-topic with no setup. |

### Body (10 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | Clear structure; each slide carries a single take-home message; content per slide is digestible. |
| 7 | Good | Mostly clear structure; a few slides are overloaded or lack a clear point. |
| 4 | Developing | Structure is hard to follow; many slides cram multiple ideas or none. |
| 0 | Missing | No discernible structure. |

### Conclusion (5 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Excellent | Summarizes the key insights and lands a strong, memorable final message. |
| 3 | Good | Summarizes but trails off; no distinct final takeaway. |
| 0 | Missing | Ends abruptly with no conclusion. |

### Clarity and Conciseness (10 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | Clear and concise throughout; no walls of text or illegible low-resolution images. |
| 7 | Good | Mostly clear; occasional dense text or a low-quality image. |
| 4 | Developing | Recurrent dense slides or unreadable graphics. |
| 0 | Missing | Consistently unclear. |

### Slide Design (10 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | Visually appealing; good balance of text, images, and white space; high-quality, legible graphics. |
| 7 | Good | Functional design with some cluttered or bare slides. |
| 4 | Developing | Design actively hinders comprehension. |
| 0 | Missing | No attention to design. |

### Collaboration (10 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | Balanced contributions across the group, evident in the shared doc/presentation history and consistent with the contribution statements. |
| 7 | Good | Everyone contributed but noticeably unevenly. |
| 4 | Developing | One or two members carried the project; others' contributions are hard to identify. |
| 0 | Missing | No evidence of collaboration. |

### Individual Contribution (10 pts, per student)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Excellent | Confidential statement accurately and specifically describes the student's own contribution and the group's division of work; consistent with the group's account. |
| 7 | Good | Statement submitted but vague about what the student actually did. |
| 4 | Developing | Statement minimal or inconsistent with other evidence. |
| 0 | Missing | No statement submitted. |

### Time Management and Communication (5 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Excellent | Under 10 minutes; efficient coverage; clear articulation, good pacing, engages the audience. |
| 3 | Good | Slightly over/under time, or pacing issues (rushed ending, long tangents). |
| 0 | Missing | Far outside the time window or disengaged delivery. |

### Audience Engagement (5 pts, per student)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Excellent | Present and engaged during other groups' presentations on both days. |
| 3 | Good | Missed part of the presentations, or present but not paying attention. |
| 0 | Missing | Absent or disengaged during other presentations. |

### Extra Credit: Novelty (up to 5 pts)
| Pts | Level | Description |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Excellent | Presents genuinely creative insights, framings, or approaches not found in standard materials. |
| 2 | Good | Some fresh angle beyond the obvious treatment. |
| 0 | None | Standard treatment. |
